about: Per-variable expectations for the server-baseline rules, so no rule hard-codes one. Every entry is written here in our own words with the vendor page it rests on; nothing is copied. `sqlens_expectation` may be null, which means the value is worth READING but not worth judging — usually because the right answer depends on the deployment. `changeable` is load-bearing rather than descriptive: an `initdb` variable cannot be altered afterwards, so a rule about one must report a fact to plan around instead of proposing a change that is impossible.

entries.note: utf8mb3 cannot store the 4-byte range at all — emoji and much of CJK — so a server defaulting to it silently truncates or rejects on insert rather than at schema time. Measured on 8.4.10: @@session.character_set_server answers utf8mb4, so it is Global+Session and dynamic — it was recorded as restart-only in error.
A non-InnoDB default silently produces tables without transactions or foreign keys, and nothing in a migration says so.
OFF revives the pre-5.6 semantics where a TIMESTAMP column silently gains NOT NULL and an auto-update clause nobody wrote.

Records every statement the server receives, verbatim and unredacted, because it is a debugging tool rather than an audit trail: CREATE USER ... IDENTIFIED BY goes in with the password, and so does any value interpolated into SQL rather than bound. Off is the vendor default and the expectation, because the variable is meant to be on for minutes while somebody is looking at something -- a server that has it on is almost always one where that was forgotten, and the cost grows silently with uptime. Recorded as reload rather than session: it is GLOBAL-only, so SET GLOBAL moves it without downtime but no session may.

WHERE the general query log lands when general_log is on -- the other half of that setting, and the half that decides who can read what it recorded. Deliberately NOT judged: a path is not safe or unsafe by itself. Whether it sits beside the data directory, on a shared volume, or inside something a log shipper sweeps up is a fact about the host, and a rule claiming it from the value alone would be claiming more than it read. Recorded because a finding about general_log is more actionable when it can name the file. Measured on 8.4.10: VARIABLE_SOURCE=COMPILED, so the value read there was the vendor default; the default itself is host-derived, which is why it is written as a shape rather than a string.

COMPACT caps an index prefix at 767 bytes, which a utf8mb4 column of 191 characters already reaches — the limit surfaces as a failed migration, not as a warning. Measured on 8.4.10: it has NO session scope at all — reading @@session.innodb_default_row_format answers ERROR 1238, "is a GLOBAL variable" — so it was recorded as session-changeable in error.

Governs whether the server may ask the CLIENT to send it a file, which is the opposite direction from what the name suggests: LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE has the server name a path and the client read it off its own disk. Off is the vendor default on 8.4 and the expectation here, because the capability costs an application nothing to lose -- a data-import job that genuinely needs it can enable it for the one session that does. Recorded as reload rather than session: it is a GLOBAL-only dynamic variable, so SET GLOBAL changes it without downtime but no individual session may set it, and a remediation offering a per-session fix would be advice nobody can follow.

No expectation on purpose: the right value depends on the deployment's filesystem, and it CANNOT be changed after initialization — a rule about it can only report a mismatch between environments, never a fix.

Decides whether a connection that did NOT negotiate encryption is refused -- which is a different question from whether encryption is available. MySQL 8 negotiates TLS by default and most clients take it, so a server with this OFF usually looks encrypted from the inside: every connection somebody checks is one that happened to negotiate it. The expectation is ON while the vendor default is OFF, and that gap is deliberate: the default leaves the guarantee to every client, and a client whose TLS setup silently failed connects in the clear with nothing raised. Note the limit the rule states too -- several managed providers enforce transport at a proxy outside the server configuration, and this variable reads OFF on such a server.

The variable whose naive reading is INVERTED, which is why the rule classifies it instead of comparing it to this expectation. MySQL writes the switched-off state as the four-character STRING "NULL" and the unrestricted state as the EMPTY string, so an is_null(), an empty() or a ?: 'unset' swaps the two ends of the scale: the safest server reads as unconfigured and the most dangerous one reads as nothing set. Measured on 8.4.10 through both read paths. A PATH is a third, legitimate state and must not be reported, so a straight comparison against the expectation below would fail every deliberately confined server; the expectation records the hardened target for the remediation text, not the test. Read-only at run time -- it moves in my.cnf and takes a restart.

Four independent guards live in this one variable, so four rules judge it — one flag each, because a project may legitimately accept one and want the others, and a single id would let one ignore entry silence all four. Expressed as a comma-separated set rather than a nested object: the file's key allowlist is closed, and a new key would be silently inert until the value object learned to map it. Without STRICT_TRANS_TABLES an out-of-range or over-long value is truncated and the statement succeeds — data loss reported as success. Laravel sets sql_mode per session from the connection's strict flag, so the GLOBAL value is what a rule must read.

SYSTEM ties stored and converted times to the host's zone, so the same database answers differently after a server move — and named zones need the timezone tables loaded, which a fresh install does not have.

Which TLS protocol versions the server will negotiate. Measured on 8.4.10: TLSv1.2,TLSv1.3 with VARIABLE_SOURCE=COMPILED -- 8.4 removed TLSv1 and TLSv1.1 outright, so the vendor default carries no deprecated version and the common finding on older servers cannot occur here. NOT judged for now, because the honest check is a SET comparison rather than a value comparison: an operator may legitimately narrow this to TLSv1.3 alone, which is stronger and would read as a mismatch against any single expected string. A rule wanting to judge it needs set semantics first; until then this entry exists so the value is READ and reportable rather than absent.
The session zone decides what timestamptz renders as and how a bare timestamp is interpreted on input; a server on local time makes two application servers disagree about the same row.
On since 18 by default. It cannot be turned on later without re-initializing the cluster, so a rule about it reports a fact to plan around rather than a change to make.
A stricter default changes the failure mode of every transaction the application never marked: serializable turns concurrency into retryable errors the code may not handle.
On at the server level makes every write fail with 25006 — sometimes deliberate on a replica, which is why this is reported with the instance's role rather than judged alone.

Which aspects of connection setup the server logs. The type is the finding here: through 17 this was a boolean defaulting to off, and in 18 it is a STRING taking a list of aspects (receipt, authentication, authorization, setup_durations) defaulting to empty. Measured on 18.4: vartype string, boot_val empty, context superuser-backend -- so a configuration reload applies it to new backends and a superuser may also request it per connection, but a running session cannot change its own. An expectation written from the pre-18 documentation would have been the string 'off', which this server would never report. No expectation is recorded because more logging here is an audit trail rather than a leak: unlike log_statement it records who connected, not what they ran, so the right amount is a deployment's decision and not a property of the variable.

Decides which statements the server writes to its log verbatim. Measured on 18.4: boot value none, enum {none,ddl,mod,all}, context superuser -- so it is dynamic and a running server can be switched to full logging without a restart, which is exactly how it ends up on and forgotten. No expectation is recorded because there is no single right value: ddl is ordinary, and all is right for the few minutes somebody is watching. What makes it a finding is the value together with the environment, and an environment is not a property of a variable.

Decides the hash every password set from now on is stored with -- not the ones already stored, which are reported per account. The vendor default has been the hardened value since 14, so this is quiet on a stock server and fires only on one somebody weakened. Recorded as session because the parameter has context user: measured on 18.4, an ordinary SET changes it, so the server's value is the default new connections inherit rather than a rule they cannot break. That same measurement is why a rule here must read reset_val -- with such a SET in place pg_settings answers setting = md5 beside reset_val = scram-sha-256. The parameter is an enum with exactly two values: 18.4 answers a third with `invalid value ... Available values: md5, scram-sha-256`.

Whether the server offers TLS at all -- not whether it insists on it. Off is the vendor default and the expectation here is on, and that gap is the finding: with ssl off no connection can be encrypted, including the ones somebody checks, and a careful client cannot make up for it because insisting on TLS fails the connection rather than securing it. Recorded as reload because the setting has context sighup: a configuration reload picks it up, no restart and no downtime. Measured on PostgreSQL 18: setting off, boot_val off, context sighup.

The cipher list the server offers for TLSv1.2 and below. Measured on 18.4: setting and boot_val both HIGH:MEDIUM:+3DES:!aNULL, source default, context sighup -- so a reload applies a change and no restart is needed. No expectation is recorded, and the reason is the shape of the value rather than a lack of opinion: this is a SET, and a server that narrows it is stricter, not wrong. Compared against any single expected string, the safest configurations in the field would read as the finding. It is recorded so a TLS finding can name what the server actually offers instead of describing it in the abstract.

The oldest TLS version this server will still negotiate. The vendor default is already TLSv1.2, so an entry here is not about repairing a bad default -- it is about noticing a server that was moved BELOW it, usually years ago for one client that no longer exists. TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are withdrawn (RFC 8996) and their weaknesses are downgrade-reachable: a server that still accepts them gives an active attacker something to negotiate down to, and the connection still reports as encrypted. The comparison is ordered, never lexical -- the value is an enum whose declared order IS the ordering, and a string compare would rank TLSv1.10 below TLSv1.2 if such a name ever existed. Measured on PostgreSQL 18.4: setting TLSv1.2, boot_val TLSv1.2, vartype enum, enumvals {TLSv1,TLSv1.1,TLSv1.2,TLSv1.3}, context sighup.
Off makes a backslash an escape character inside ordinary string literals, which changes what a stored value MEANS and is a classic injection surface.
